## Where we left off {.smaller .proof}

```cpp
void selectionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 0; i < C.size(); i++) {
        int m = idxOfMin(C, i);
        swap(C, m, i);
    }
}
```

**Thm.** &nbsp; After `selectionSort(C)` returns, `C` is a permutation of $C_0$
and $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[n-1]$.

\

**Loop invariant.** &nbsp; $P(i)$, at the start of iteration $i$: \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$ \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B.**&nbsp; $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]$ \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]$

::: notes
Where Monday ended. Read the theorem, read $P(i)$, then go.

Two things worth re-saying before resuming, because they are the reasons the
rest of the proof works:

- **$C_0$ is the array we were handed.** Clause A is the first half of the
  theorem, carried through every iteration. Sortedness alone would not say the
  values are still ours -- zeroing the array leaves it sorted.
- **Clause C is not in the theorem.** It is there purely to make restoration go
  through. That was Monday's punchline: the invariant has to be *stronger* than
  what you are trying to prove.

Then: initialization, restoration, termination. Three obligations, and we are
about to discharge them in order.
:::

## Initialization {.smaller .proof}

::: {.invariant}
**P(i)** at the start of iteration $i$:

**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$

**B.**&nbsp; $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]$

**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]$
:::


```cpp
void selectionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 0; i < C.size(); i++) {
        int m = idxOfMin(C, i);
        swap(C, m, i);
    }
}
```
Check that the loop invariant holds at the start of the loop:

($i =$ \_\_\_)

::: notes
Blank for annotation. All three clauses, and all three are easy:

- **permutation** -- nothing has run, so `C` still holds exactly what it held
  on entry. The identity is a permutation.
- **sorted** -- `C[0..-1]` is empty, and the empty sequence is sorted.
- **the 0 smallest** -- vacuous; there is no $k$ with $0 \le k < 0$.

Do not rush past the empty-range cases. Students distrust them, and this is the
cheapest place to get comfortable with "vacuously true".
:::

## Restoration {.smaller .proof}

::: {.invariant}
**P(i)** at the start of iteration $i$:

**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$

**B.**&nbsp; $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]$

**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]$
:::


```cpp
void selectionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 0; i < C.size(); i++) {
        int m = idxOfMin(C, i);
        swap(C, m, i);
    }
}
```

Assume the invariant at the start of iteration $i$. 

Run the body:

&nbsp;&nbsp;Line 3: 

&nbsp;&nbsp;Line 4:

Check the invariants:

&nbsp;&nbsp;A.

&nbsp;&nbsp;B.

&nbsp;&nbsp;C.

::: notes
Blank for annotation. Set up the step before proving anything.

By Lemma (`idxOfMin`), $i \le m < n$ and `C[m]` is the smallest value in
`C[i..n-1]`. The call does not modify `C`.

By Lemma (`swap`), afterwards `C'[i] = C[m]`, `C'[m] = C[i]`, and every other
entry is untouched.

**Permutation** falls out here: a swap is a transposition, and a composition of
permutations is a permutation. One line, then move on -- the interesting work
is the next slide.

Worth pointing at: this proof *uses* Wednesday's result. That is what proving
small things buys you.
:::


## Termination {.smaller .proof}

::: {.invariant}
**P(i)** at the start of iteration $i$:

**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$

**B.**&nbsp; $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]$

**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]$
:::


```cpp
void selectionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 0; i < C.size(); i++) {
        int m = idxOfMin(C, i);
        swap(C, m, i);
    }
}
```

Does the loop stop?

What is the state when it does?

::: notes
Stops: $i$ rises by one against a fixed bound, so after $n$ iterations the
guard fails.

At exit $i = n$, so the invariant reads: `C[0..n-1]` is sorted and holds the
$n$ smallest values -- which is the whole array. Sorted. That is the theorem.

Note the second clause does nothing at all at this point. It existed only to
get us here, and then it retires.
:::
## A mystery function {.smaller}

```cpp
void ________ (vector<int>& C, int loc) {
// assumes C[0..loc-1] is sorted, loc valid
    int j = loc;
    while (j > 0 && C[j-1] > C[j]) {
        swap(C, j-1, j);
        j--;
    }
}
```

|  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4 |  5 |  6 |  7 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|  8 | 14 | 26 | 32 | 19 | 35 |  2 | 10 |

What does it do? &nbsp;&nbsp; How long does it take? &nbsp;&nbsp; Is it correct?

::: notes
Trace it with `loc = 4`, the 19. It swaps left past 32, past 26, stops at 14.
The sorted prefix grew by one.

Name: `slide`, or `insert`. It takes one element and slides it back into a
sorted prefix.

Time: worst case `loc` swaps -- the element belongs at the front. Best case
zero -- it is already in place. Worth noticing now, because it is where
insertion sort's two cases come from.

Note the precondition on line 2. Everything this function does is wrong if
`C[0..loc-1]` is not already sorted. That is the first time a comment has been
load-bearing.
:::

## Is `slide` correct? {.smaller .proof}

```cpp
void slide (vector<int>& C, int loc) {
// assumes C[0..loc-1] is sorted, loc valid
    int j = loc;
    while (j > 0 && C[j-1] > C[j]) {
        swap(C, j-1, j);
        j--;
    }
}
```

**Thm.** &nbsp; If `C[0..loc-1]` is sorted, then afterwards `C` is a permutation
of $C_0$ and `C[0..loc]` is sorted.

- Variable: $j$, from \_\_\_ down to \_\_\_
- Loop invariant $Q(j)$, at the top of the test: \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**A.**&nbsp; `C` is a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of $C_0$ \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B.**&nbsp; `C[0..`\_\_\_`]` is sorted, and `C[`\_\_\_`..loc]` is sorted \
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < j} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{j < k \le \mathit{loc}} C[k]$

::: notes
Blanks: $j$ runs from `loc` down; **permutation**; `C[0..j-1]` and `C[j..loc]`.

Say what the invariant is picturing: one value is in flight at position $j$,
and everything on either side of it is already in its final relative order.

- **A** -- the body is a `swap` and nothing else, so this is free. *This is what
  we bought by not using a temp variable.* With `temp`, mid-loop the array holds
  a duplicate and is missing a value, and clause A is simply false until the
  last line.
- **B** -- `C[0..j-1]` is an untouched piece of the sorted prefix. `C[j..loc]`
  is sorted because the guard only swapped when `C[j-1] > C[j]`: everything we
  pushed up is bigger than the value we are carrying.
- **C** -- the strengthening clause, exactly as in selection sort. Second time
  this move has come up, so name it again.
:::

## `slide`, continued {.smaller .proof}

::: {.invariant}
**Q(j)** at the top of the test:

**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$

**B.**&nbsp; $C[0..j-1]$ and $C[j..\mathit{loc}]$ are each sorted

**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < j} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{j < k \le \mathit{loc}} C[k]$
:::


```cpp
void slide (vector<int>& C, int loc) {
// assumes C[0..loc-1] is sorted, loc valid
    int j = loc;
    while (j > 0 && C[j-1] > C[j]) {
        swap(C, j-1, j);
        j--;
    }
}
```

Initialization: &nbsp; $j =$ \_\_\_

\

Restoration:

::: notes
Initialization: $j = loc$. A is trivial, B is the precondition plus a one-element
suffix, C is vacuous on the right.

Restoration: assume $Q(j)$ and that the guard passed, so `C[j-1] > C[j]`. The
body swaps them and decrements. A survives because a swap is a transposition.
B survives because the value we pushed up is bigger than the one we are
carrying. C survives because both pieces only lost and gained the one element
in flight.

Termination is the interesting one and gets its own slide.
:::

## `slide`, termination {.smaller .proof}

::: {.invariant}
**Q(j)** at the top of the test:

**A.**&nbsp; $C$ is a permutation of $C_0$

**B.**&nbsp; $C[0..j-1]$ and $C[j..\mathit{loc}]$ are each sorted

**C.**&nbsp; $\max_{0 \le k < j} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{j < k \le \mathit{loc}} C[k]$
:::


```cpp
void slide (vector<int>& C, int loc) {
// assumes C[0..loc-1] is sorted, loc valid
    int j = loc;
    while (j > 0 && C[j-1] > C[j]) {
        swap(C, j-1, j);
        j--;
    }
}
```

The loop exits when \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ &nbsp; **or** &nbsp; \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

Case 1:

\

Case 2:

::: notes
**Two ways out, and they are not the same argument.** The guard is
`j > 0 && C[j-1] > C[j]`, so it fails if *either* conjunct fails.

**Case 1: `C[j-1] <= C[j]`.** The value in flight is no smaller than its left
neighbour. B already gives `C[0..j-1]` sorted and `C[j..loc]` sorted, and this
is exactly the one comparison joining them. Plus C, so everything left of $j$
is $\le$ everything right of it. `C[0..loc]` is sorted.

**Case 2: $j = 0$.** There is nothing to the left at all. B's first piece is
empty, so B alone gives it -- no join needed, and C is vacuous.

Either way `C[0..loc]` is sorted, and A says the values are still ours. That is
the theorem.

Students want to handle only Case 1. Make them say why Case 2 is not a gap --
and notice that it is the case that actually happens when the element belongs
at the front, which is insertion sort's worst case.
:::

## Insertion sort {.smaller}

```cpp
void insertionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 1; i < C.size(); i++)
        slide(C, i);
}
```

|  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4 |  5 |  6 |  7 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 14 | 26 |  8 | 19 | 35 |  2 | 10 |

Worst case running time:

|  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4 |  5 |  6 |  7 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|    |    |    |    |    |    |    |    |

Best case?

|  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4 |  5 |  6 |  7 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|    |    |    |    |    |    |    |    |

::: notes
Two lines, because `slide` did the work. Trace a couple of iterations on the
top array before going near running time.

Worst: fill the blank row reversed -- every element slides the whole way.
$1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = \Theta(n^2)$.

Best: fill it already sorted. Every call to `slide` tests once and stops.
$\Theta(n)$.

**Stop and make the comparison.** Selection sort's best and worst were both
$\Theta(n^2)$, because `idxOfMin` always scans everything. Insertion sort's
differ by a growth rate -- the first algorithm all term where the data changes
the answer.

Worth asking out loud: if you knew your input was nearly sorted, which would
you reach for?
:::

## Insertion sort --- correctness {.smaller .proof}

```cpp
void insertionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 1; i < C.size(); i++)
        slide(C, i);
}
```

|  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4 |  5 |  6 |  7 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|    |    |    |    |    |    |    |    |

Correctness proof ---

- Variable: $i \in \{1 \ldots n\}$
- Loop invariant: at start of arb iter $i$, `C` is a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of the input, and `C[0..`\_\_\_`]` is sorted
- Initialization: $i =$ \_\_\_ . &nbsp; `C[0..`\_\_\_`]` sorted?
- Restoration: assume LI holds at start of iteration $i$.
- Termination: $i =$ \_\_\_\_\_ , LI gives

::: notes
Blanks: **permutation** ... `C[0..i-1]` ... $i=1$, `C[0..0]` ... $i=n$.

Two clauses only -- compare selection sort, which also needed "and holds the
$i$ smallest". Insertion sort does not, because it never claims the prefix is
final; placed elements still move. The invariant follows from what the
algorithm guarantees, not from the theorem.

Restoration: this is now one line, by the Lemma. `slide`'s precondition is
`C[0..i-1]` sorted, which is exactly clause B of the invariant. Its conclusion
is that `C` is still a permutation and `C[0..i]` is sorted -- which is $P(i+1)$.
Nothing else to do.

Say how short that was next to selection sort, and why: the work went into
`slide`, and the loop took three lines because the building block was already
proved. Same shape as `idxOfMin` and selection sort on Monday. **Prove the
small thing, then the big thing is easy.**
:::
